turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. Smith, my wife actually set this up. I'm here because... well, it's about the environmental modeling contract I'm working on right now. I'm pretty sure the people on that contract have been tracking my revisions. They keep planting errors in the datasets to make it look like I can’t lead the work. 

Which is just... I mean, I've been doing this kind of math since the 80s. I remember when we had to use those big floppy disks for everything. Did you ever use those? The really flimsy five-and-a-quarter inch ones, not the hard plastic ones. I had a whole stack of them on my desk back when we lived out in Denver. Beautiful city, Denver, but the altitude really did a number on my sinuses. I couldn't breathe through my nose half the winter, had to buy this special humidifier that just hummed all night long. 

But anyway, my wife, and even the junior analysts at the office, they keep telling me it’s just version-control mistakes. Like I don't know how the software works or something. But I know what I'm seeing in the data.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that colleagues are tracking his revisions and planting errors to sabotage him, despite his wife and junior analysts providing contradictory evidence (version-control mistakes).
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and derailment, wandering from the topic of his work contract to floppy disks, living in Denver, the altitude, and a humidifier, before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear any voices or sounds that other people around you don't seem to hear?
turns.patient_response: Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. Just the usual office noise, you know? The hum of the servers, people typing. Although, speaking of typing, my old keyboard... I had this mechanical one, an IBM Model M. Best keyboard ever made. The keys had this incredible spring to them, made this loud, satisfying clack every time you hit a letter. It drove my old cubicle mate, Gary, absolutely up the wall. Gary was a strange guy, always eating these little tins of sardines for lunch. The smell was just awful, it would linger in the breakroom for hours. I tried spraying this citrus air freshener I got from the dollar store, but it just made it smell like lemon-scented fish. We finally had to complain to HR about it. But no, no voices or anything out of the ordinary. Just... just the data.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the topic of office noise to keyboards, a former coworker, sardines, and air freshener.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or any sounds out of the ordinary.

turns.doctor_question: When you are speaking, do you often find that your thoughts get jumbled or that you have trouble keeping your train of thought on track?
turns.patient_response:
Jumbled? No, not at all. My thoughts are perfectly organized. I mean, you have to be organized to do the kind of mathematical modeling I do. It's all about logical progression, keeping your train of thought on a very strict track. 

Speaking of tracks, we used to take the Amtrak down to Chicago for these big data conferences back in the late 90s. The dining car on those trains was actually quite nice, they had these little heavy silver coffee pots. Real silver, not that cheap aluminum stuff they use everywhere now. I actually bought one at an antique shop years later because it reminded me of those trips. I keep it on the shelf in my home office, right next to my old calculus textbooks. My wife keeps threatening to donate those books to the local library, but you can't just give away good reference material, you know? The fundamentals of calculus don't change, even if the software does. I told her, if she touches my Thomas' Calculus, I'm throwing out her gardening magazines. 

But, no, my thoughts don't get jumbled. I know exactly what I'm doing and what I'm saying. It's the people messing with my contract who are confused, not me.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies having jumbled thoughts, but their response clearly demonstrates disorganized speech through tangentiality and loose associations (jumping from 'train of thought' to Amtrak trains, coffee pots, and calculus textbooks).

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel that other people in your life, besides those working on your contract, are also conspiring against you or trying to undermine you in some way?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, no, nobody else. It’s strictly the people on the contract. My wife doesn't really understand the data, but she's not trying to undermine me or anything. She's mostly just focused on her gardening right now. 

In fact, she's got it in her head this week that we need to build these new raised beds for her heirloom tomatoes. We had to drive all the way out to this specialized nursery on County Road 9 just to get the right compost blend. The guy who owns it, Frank, he's been running that place since... oh, it has to be 1992. He actually sold me this incredible vintage wheelbarrow he had sitting out behind the main greenhouse. Solid steel tub, heavy ash wood handles. You really don't see craftsmanship like that anymore, everything you buy at the hardware store now is just cheap plastic that cracks in a year. 

I actually spent my whole Sunday just sanding down those old handles and treating them with boiled linseed oil. Have you ever worked with linseed oil? It has this very distinct, rich smell to it. It immediately brought me back to my grandfather’s garage when I was a boy. He used to spend hours out there building these elaborate wooden grandfather clocks, the kind with the really heavy brass weights...

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient reaffirms his fixed delusional belief that the people working on his contract are conspiring against him, even while denying that others are involved.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, drifting far from the original question into a long, unrelated tangent about gardening, a vintage wheelbarrow, linseed oil, and his grandfather's clocks.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your daily habits or the way you carry out routine tasks, such as how you dress, bathe, or organize your personal space?
turns.patient_response:
Changes? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I keep my routine very strict. I get up at the same time, shower, put on a clean shirt. I always wear those button-down Oxford shirts, you know? The light blue ones. I've been buying the exact same brand from this catalog for... gosh, it has to be fifteen years. 

Though the shipping takes absolutely forever now. I remember back in the early 2000s, you'd order something from a catalog and it would be on your porch in three days. The mail carriers were just more dedicated back then. Our old mailman, Arthur, he used to actually walk all the way up our steep driveway, rain or shine. He had this incredible vintage leather mail satchel. He said it was issued to him in 1978, and the leather had this beautiful, rich patina on it from all the weather. 

I actually tried to buy a bag just like it on eBay a few years ago to hold my modeling schematics, but the auction got sniped at the last second. People use these automated bidding bots now, it completely ruins the spirit of a live auction. It's just algorithms fighting other algorithms over the internet, no human element left at all. I mean, if you're going to write a script to bid for you, at least randomize the interval so it doesn't look so obvious to the server logs. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, my daily habits. No, no changes there. Everything is just how I like it.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from their daily routine to shirts, mail carriers, eBay, and bidding bots before losing track of the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient explicitly denies any changes or deterioration in their daily habits, dressing, or bathing routines, stating they keep a strict routine.
